config.title: Lippincott Path Ch6 – Developmental & Genetic Diseases
config.subtitle: Developmental and genetic pathology: cystic fibrosis, morphogenesis errors, and teratogenesis

questions.stem: A 4-year-old boy is admitted to the hospital with pneumonia and respiratory distress. The nurses report that the child's bowel movements are greasy and have a pungent odor. A sweat-chloride test is positive. Which of the following mechanisms of disease is the most likely cause of steatorrhea in this child?
questions.explanation: This child has cystic fibrosis (CF), confirmed by positive sweat-chloride test. In CF, viscous mucus obstructs pancreatic ducts, preventing delivery of lipases and proteases to the duodenum. Lack of pancreatic enzyme secretion causes malabsorption of fats, leading to steatorrhea—greasy, foul-smelling stools. All pathologic consequences of CF stem from abnormally thick mucus secretions produced by defective chloride channel function. Bacterial overgrowth (B) and abnormal dietary intake (A) are not the primary cause in CF.
keypoints: ⭐ CF causes exocrine pancreatic insufficiency → lack of lipase/protease → steatorrhea
All CF complications stem from abnormally viscous mucus blocking ductal systems
⭐ Positive sweat-chloride test (>60 mEq/L) is diagnostic of CF
CF affects pancreas, lungs, intestines, liver, and reproductive tract

questions.stem: The patient described in Question 11 carries mutations in the gene that encodes which of the following types of protein?
questions.explanation: The CF gene encodes CFTR (cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator), a member of the ATP-binding cassette family of membrane transporter proteins that functions as a chloride ion channel in epithelial cells. Chloride secretion by mucous-secreting epithelia controls parallel fluid secretion and, consequently, mucus viscosity. Defective CFTR leads to thick, dehydrated mucus. CF is the most common lethal autosomal recessive disorder in white populations, with an incidence of 1 in 2,500 newborns.
keypoints: ⭐ CFTR is a chloride ion channel encoded by the CFTR gene on chromosome 7
CFTR belongs to the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter superfamily
⭐ CF is the most common lethal autosomal recessive disease in whites (1:2,500 births)
Defective chloride secretion → reduced fluid secretion → viscous mucus

questions.stem: The mother of a newborn boy is alarmed that her baby regurgitates at every feeding. An endoscopic examination reveals that the child's esophagus is almost completely occluded. This finding represents an example of which of the following errors of morphogenesis?
questions.explanation: Atresia refers to defects caused by incomplete formation of a lumen. Many hollow organs originate as solid strands of cells whose centers are programmed to die (apoptosis), forming a central lumen. Esophageal atresia results when this canalization is incomplete, causing partial or complete luminal occlusion. Aplasia (A) means absence of an organ. Dysplasia (C) refers to abnormal cellular organization. A dysraphic anomaly (D) involves failure of neural tube closure. Ectopia (E) means displacement of tissue to an abnormal location.
keypoints: ⭐ Atresia = incomplete formation of a hollow organ's lumen (failure of canalization)
Esophageal atresia often co-occurs with tracheoesophageal fistula (TEF)
Aplasia = complete absence of an organ or tissue
⭐ Hollow organs form by canalization of solid cellular cords; failure → atresia

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman presents for a pregnancy test. She recalls drinking heavily during the week in which she may have conceived. What is the most likely consequence of toxic exposure to the conceptus during early (preimplantation) development?
questions.explanation: During the preimplantation stage, all blastomeres are totipotent and interchangeable. If a toxin damages some blastomeres, the remaining cells can compensate and development proceeds normally. However, if the damage is extensive, the entire conceptus dies—often passing unnoticed as a slightly late or heavy menstrual period. This is the 'all-or-none' principle of preimplantation toxicology. Specific malformations (neural tube defects, cardiac defects) require organ-specific embryonic development that occurs after implantation.
keypoints: ⭐ Preimplantation toxic exposure follows the 'all-or-none' principle: death or normal development
Blastomeres are totipotent; surviving cells compensate for damaged ones
Specific teratogenic malformations require post-implantation organogenesis
⭐ Neural tube defects occur during weeks 3-4; cardiac defects during weeks 3-7 post-conception
